e.t: This Hebrew word means “Bel,” functioning as a proper name rather than a general description. It occurs three times in the Old Testament corpus: once in Isaiah and twice in Jeremiah. The word appears in passages that speak about Bel and describe actions or statements concerning him, so its basic role is to identify a particular named figure. Its precise significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

Beeshterah is the name of a place. This Hebrew word appears once in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, and its recorded English rendering is “Beeshterah.” It functions as a proper place name rather than a general description or action word. It occurs in Joshua 21:27; without the surrounding verse text, the name itself identifies the location but does not by itself explain the passage’s larger significance.

This Hebrew word refers to the Berites, a people or group named in the Old Testament. It functions as a proper group designation rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The word appears once in the Hebrew Bible, in 2 Samuel 20:14, and its English rendering is “Berites.” Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word itself identifies the group without providing further detail about its origin, character, or role in that passage.

The Hebrew word means “shocks,” functioning as a noun. It occurs four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Exodus, Judges, and Job. Its repeated use in these passages supports a concrete term rather than an abstract idea. The word’s precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its ordinary lexical sense is the noun “shocks.”

This Hebrew verb expresses the idea of coming to an end or reaching completion. It can describe something that ceases, ends, or is brought to its intended completion. In the Hebrew Bible, it occurs five times, all in the Psalms, where its use includes the ending or completion of a matter. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

e.t: Gath is a proper name identifying a place in the Old Testament. It is rendered consistently as “Gath,” rather than functioning as an ordinary descriptive word. The name appears 32 times in the Hebrew Old Testament and is associated with people, movement, speech, and conflict involving that place. Its references include Joshua, Samuel, Kings, Chronicles, and Micah, showing that Gath remains a recognizable location across several historical periods. The surrounding verse determines what is happening there in each passage.

“Fishers” refers to people engaged in catching fish. It is a plural noun naming those who do this work, rather than the fish or the act itself. In the Hebrew Old Testament, the word occurs twice, and both occurrences are rendered “fishers.” It appears in Jeremiah 16:16 and Ezekiel 47:10, showing its ordinary use for people who catch fish. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word refers to something named in Deuteronomy 23:1, but its precise ordinary meaning cannot be established from the available lexical information. It appears only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in that verse, so there are no other occurrences to clarify its use. The verse text and an approved meaning term are not available here; therefore, no more specific definition should be assigned without adding information beyond this record.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to a “decree”—an authoritative order or ruling issued for people to follow. It can describe a command associated with a king or with God. In its 22 Old Testament occurrences, it functions as the thing announced, given, or observed, rather than the person who acts. Its use in Esther especially highlights decrees that govern public action and can carry serious consequences.

It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Ezekiel 21:15, so Scripture provides only one recorded use for observing its normal sense. Here, “point” is the clearest supported meaning for this word, while the surrounding verse is needed to explain its particular significance there.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to “majesty” or “glory”—the visible greatness, dignity, and splendor associated with a person or ruler. It is used especially of God’s supreme greatness, but can also describe the honor or impressive dignity granted to human rulers and displayed in creation. The word occurs 24 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing a recurring emphasis on greatness that can be possessed, displayed, or given. Its use in giving and speech contexts also connects majesty with public honor and recognition.

This Hebrew word means “here.” It functions as a location word, directing attention to a particular place or point in the immediate setting. It occurs 11 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing in passages from Genesis through Psalms. Its use can identify where someone or something is, or indicate the place being pointed out in speech. The surrounding verse determines exactly what place is meant in each occurrence.

The Hebrew word means “father.” It is a noun used to identify a male parent in relation to his child. In its Old Testament usage, it appears nine times across Ezra and Daniel, consistently carrying this basic family relationship. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on the surrounding verse, but the word itself plainly points to a father. It is found in seven Old Testament verses, including passages referring to fathers connected with the people and kings mentioned there.

e.t: “Zebulonite” is a noun identifying a person belonging to Zebulun. It functions as a people-group or tribal designation rather than describing an action, quality, or object. This Hebrew word occurs three times in the Old Testament corpus: once in Numbers and twice in Judges. In each use, it identifies someone by association with Zebulun. Its meaning is therefore a straightforward personal designation: a Zebulonite, or member of that group.

This Hebrew verb describes something that has run out, failed, or become absent. It can express a supply being exhausted, a person or thing no longer being present, or movement away, depending on the sentence. Its approved meaning clues are “about” and “fail,” with “fail” especially indicating loss or depletion. The word occurs five times in the Hebrew Old Testament, each in a different verse, so its precise force depends on what has become absent or depleted in the surrounding context.

e.t: Hotham is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in 1 Chronicles, where it identifies a person within genealogical records. The name is rendered “Hotham,” with one English spelling variation appearing in another reference. Its precise family connection belongs to the surrounding genealogical context, not to the name’s basic meaning.

e.t: This Hebrew noun refers to an “army”: an organized body of people prepared for battle. It normally identifies a collective force in accounts of conflict, military campaigns, and the strength or presence of a people. The word occurs 19 times in the Hebrew Old Testament. Its precise sense in any individual verse depends on how the surrounding passage describes that army.

Hachmoni, also rendered Hachmonite, is a Hebrew identifying name or designation. It appears twice in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, both times in 1 Chronicles. The word functions as a personal or family designation rather than expressing an action, quality, or object. Its exact significance in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the supplied renderings consistently preserve it as the name Hachmoni or the designation Hachmonite.

Hanniel is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs twice: once in Numbers 34:23 and once in 1 Chronicles 7:39. The biblical renderings identify the name as “Hanniel,” but the available information does not provide a further lexical definition or explain the name’s meaning. Its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and genealogy.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “half,” referring to one of two equal portions or divisions. It can describe something divided into two parts, or identify one portion within a larger whole. In the Old Testament, it occurs 123 times, showing regular use for measured portions and divisions. Its exact sense in a particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains one part of something separated into two portions.

e.t: Ahimelech is a personal name, referring to a particular man rather than expressing an action, quality, or general concept. In the Hebrew Old Testament, this name appears 16 times across 15 verses and is consistently rendered “Ahimelech.” The occurrences span 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, and 1 Chronicles, so the word functions as a person’s name throughout this corpus. The surrounding verse determines which mention is intended.

This Hebrew word refers to a row or rows—an ordered line or tier of items placed together. In its Old Testament usage, it describes arranged elements in furnishings and building details, including the priestly breastpiece and temple construction. It occurs 26 times in the Hebrew Bible, with the same central idea of an ordered row or tier. The surrounding passage determines exactly what objects are arranged. (Exod. 28:17; 1 Kgs. 6:36.)

This Hebrew verb expresses being “weary.” It describes a condition of exhaustion or weariness and functions as an action or state within a sentence. The word occurs 26 times in the Old Testament, showing that it is used across several kinds of passages rather than belonging to only one setting. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage. Scripture uses it in references ranging from Joshua and 2 Samuel to Psalms, Isaiah, and Malachi.

Ezekiel is a personal name, referring to the prophet Ezekiel and to another person named in 1 Chronicles. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs three times, all as a person’s name. Two occurrences are in Ezekiel, where the name identifies the prophet; another appears in 1 Chronicles. Its precise significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage, but its ordinary function is to identify a person named Ezekiel.

Jazer is a place name referring to a town or region in the Old Testament. It is not presented here as an ordinary descriptive word with a separate gloss, but as the name of a location. The name appears 13 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, beginning in Numbers and extending through Jeremiah. Scripture places Jazer among territories and towns, including areas associated with Israel’s tribal inheritance and later references to Moab. Its precise significance in any passage depends on the surrounding context and the historical setting being described.

This Hebrew word means “burning.” It describes fire in action or a burning condition, whether referring to the continuing fire on an altar or to fire pictured as bringing intense judgment. It occurs nine times in the Old Testament, including passages in Leviticus, Deuteronomy, Isaiah, and Jeremiah. Its normal sense remains centered on burning rather than on a separate abstract idea; the surrounding verse determines whether the word emphasizes the fire itself or its ongoing activity.

This Hebrew word describes something glorious or stately—marked by honor, splendor, or impressive dignity. It can refer to the distinguished appearance of a person or object, so its precise force depends on the sentence where it appears. The word occurs three times in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Judges 18:21, Psalm 45:13, and Ezekiel 23:41. In each setting, it functions as a descriptive term for something presented as impressive or dignified, rather than naming an action or a person.

e.t: The Hebrew word means “basons,” functioning as a noun for a kind of vessel. In the Old Testament data provided, it appears 12 times across six verses. Most occurrences are concentrated in 1 Chronicles and Ezra, with additional appearances in Exodus, Job, and Psalms. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding Hebrew sentence, but its clearest supported ordinary sense is “basons.”

This Hebrew verb means “bow” or “bowed,” describing the act of bending or lowering oneself. It can refer to physically bending at the knees or body, including kneeling before God or another person. The word occurs 36 times in the Old Testament, showing a repeated picture of people or creatures lowering themselves. Its exact force—whether simple physical movement, submission, or reverence—depends on the surrounding verse and its subject.

Lebonah is a proper name, preserved in English as “Lebonah” rather than translated into an ordinary descriptive word. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Judges 21:19. Because the available wording identifies it only by this name and does not provide the surrounding verse text, its precise role in that passage must be understood from the context of Judges 21. Lexically, the word functions as a name, not as a general term describing an action, quality, or object.

e.t: This Hebrew noun refers to a “commandment.” It functions as a noun, identifying the commandment as something that can be given, kept, or discussed. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in Esther. Its uses center on an authoritative command and the requirement to follow it. The word is also associated with a command being issued and observed, showing that it names the command itself rather than the action of obeying it.

Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, the word’s precise reference in that passage cannot be explained further. Its basic sense remains focused and concrete: it identifies ends as distinct parts of an object or structure, rather than describing an action, quality, or person.

The word can function within statements about how many remain or how long something will last, while the precise force in each passage comes from its surrounding words.

It is used of a specific place rather than as a general description or action. The name occurs 13 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including passages in Genesis, Joshua, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, and 1 Chronicles.

It functions as a noun for the governing realm itself, whether the kingdom belongs to a human king or is spoken of in relation to God’s rule. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs nine times, including several descriptions of territories in Joshua and a reference to Saul’s kingdom in 1 Samuel. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding context.

e.t: This Hebrew noun refers to a “portion,” meaning a share or designated part given to someone. It can describe what people receive or are assigned, including provisions connected with service and worship. Its uses also appear in settings of giving, where a portion is provided to those who have a recognized responsibility. The word occurs seven times in the Old Testament, in Chronicles, Nehemiah, and Psalms. The surrounding context determines whether the portion is material, assigned, or received as one’s share.

This Hebrew word refers to “Memphis,” a place name. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Hosea 9:6, so its meaning is geographical rather than a general quality, action, or description. The available usage presents it as a named place, but the surrounding verse text is not available here. Its precise significance in that verse therefore depends on the context of Hosea 9:6.

This Hebrew noun means “stall,” referring to a place where an animal is kept. It appears four times in the Old Testament, with the same central sense across references in 1 Samuel, Jeremiah, Amos, and Malachi. The word functions as a concrete noun rather than describing an action or quality. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning points to an animal’s enclosure or keeping place.

This Hebrew word means “habitation,” referring to a place where someone dwells. It names a dwelling place rather than an action or quality. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezra 7:15. The exact force of the word in that verse is determined by the surrounding sentence, but its ordinary sense remains a habitation—a settled place associated with dwelling. [No verse text supplied.]

Mithredath is a personal name, not a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears twice, both times in Ezra, and is rendered “Mithredath.” The name itself does not provide an additional lexical meaning. Context is needed to determine which person bearing this name is intended and what role that person has in either passage.

The word appears 119 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, from Genesis through Zechariah, showing that it is a recurring term for this kind of waterway. Its precise significance in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

e.t: This Hebrew noun means “soul.” It refers to the living self as Scripture speaks about people and other living creatures. The word can stand in passages concerned with life, death, desire, worship, protection, and the whole person before God. It is widely used in the Hebrew Old Testament, occurring 757 times, so its precise force is shaped by the sentence and surrounding passage. Its central idea remains the soul or living self.

This Hebrew verb means “be.” It expresses a state or condition in a sentence, describing what someone or something is or continues to be. It occurs nine times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including passages in Genesis, Psalms, Ecclesiastes, Isaiah, and Lamentations. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central function is to state being or condition.

This Hebrew word means “bay,” identifying something by a reddish-brown color. It occurs twice in the Old Testament, both times in Zechariah 6, where the English rendering “bay” is consistently recorded. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, its exact role in each sentence cannot be described further. Its basic sense remains a color description rather than a separate action, object, or spiritual concept.

This Hebrew word means “fins,” the swimming structures on fish. It functions as a noun naming a physical feature of aquatic creatures. In the Old Testament, it appears five times, all in Leviticus 11 and Deuteronomy 14, where fins are mentioned in teaching how to distinguish creatures that may or may not be eaten. The word therefore refers specifically to fins as an identifiable bodily feature, not to fish generally or to an action performed by them.

This Hebrew word means “presidents,” referring to people identified by that title. It is a noun used as a designation for governing officials rather than an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament data, it occurs five times, all in Daniel 6. The word’s basic sense is therefore a title for human officeholders called presidents; the surrounding passage determines the specific responsibilities or authority attached to them in each verse.

e.t: This Hebrew word is a proper place-name rather than an ordinary descriptive term. It identifies a location called עֵין־דֹּאר in the Old Testament, appearing six times in three verses: Joshua 17:11, 1 Samuel 28:7, and Psalm 83:10. No gloss or short definition is provided, so the deeper meaning of the name cannot be stated responsibly. Its function in these passages is to identify that particular location.

The Hebrew word means “occasion,” a noun for a circumstance connected with something that happens. It occurs three times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all in Daniel 6:4–5. Its noun function lets it identify a situation considered in relation to an action or event, rather than describe the action itself. In this limited usage, “occasion” is the clearest supported sense; the surrounding verse text would be needed to explain its specific force there.

e.t: This Hebrew verb describes an action, but its precise English meaning cannot be stated responsibly from the available lexical information. It appears only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Genesis 22:9. The word is identified as עָקַד, but no explicit definition, approved meaning term, or English rendering is available here. Its exact sense must therefore be established from the wording and surrounding context of Genesis 22:9 rather than from this lexical entry alone.

This Hebrew word describes something “sweet”—pleasant and pleasing in its quality. It is used only twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing in Proverbs 20:17 and Song of Songs 2:14. In both recorded renderings, it is translated “sweet,” giving a consistent picture of something delightful rather than harsh or unpleasant. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding context, but its ordinary sense is clear: it describes a pleasing quality that brings enjoyment.

This word means “governor,” a title for an official who exercises authority over a region or people. It functions as a noun, identifying a person who holds an administrative position. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs ten times, especially in Ezra and Daniel, where it is used as an official title. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and the responsibilities associated with that office.

This Hebrew word means “ephod,” referring to a particular named item rather than an abstract quality or action. It functions in the sentence as the term identifying that item. The word occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, once in Exodus 29:5 and once in Leviticus 8:7. Since the available passages do not include their verse text here, the word’s precise role in each sentence must be understood from its surrounding context.

e.t: Penuel is a proper name referring to a place in the Old Testament. It is rendered “Penuel” and appears ten times in eight verses, from Genesis through 1 Chronicles. The name identifies a location associated with people living there, building there, and traveling from there. It also appears in passages involving speech directed toward or concerning Penuel, showing that the word functions as a place-name rather than as a description or action. Its exact significance in any particular verse depends on that passage’s surrounding context.

This Hebrew noun refers to a hoof, the hard foot covering of an animal. It is used especially when Scripture describes animals according to their feet and identifies whether the hoof is split. In the dietary instructions, the hoof helps distinguish animals that may or may not be eaten, alongside other features such as chewing the cud. The word occurs 21 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including passages in Exodus, Leviticus, Deuteronomy, Ezekiel, Isaiah, and Zechariah. Its central meaning remains “hoof,” while the surrounding passage determines the specific animal being described.

This Hebrew verb means “open.” It describes the action of causing something to cease being closed. The word appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Daniel, and its basic sense remains consistent across those occurrences. As a verb, it points to an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The surrounding verse determines what is opened and how the action functions in that sentence.

This Hebrew word means “precept,” referring to an authoritative instruction or command given for people to follow. It functions as a noun naming such a directive rather than describing an action or feeling. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs nine times, concentrated in Isaiah 28 and appearing once in Hosea 5. Its use therefore presents a concise word for an imposed instruction, especially in passages speaking about what people are taught, required to observe, or made subject to.

This Hebrew verb means “cry.” It describes calling out aloud, often as an urgent appeal or strong expression directed toward someone who can hear. The word appears 55 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so it represents a recurring way people express their need, distress, or appeal. Its precise force in any passage depends on the surrounding words and situation, but the central idea remains a voiced cry rather than a quiet thought or feeling.

This Hebrew noun means “hornet,” naming a stinging insect. It occurs three times in the Old Testament corpus, in Exodus, Deuteronomy, and Joshua. In each occurrence, the word identifies the hornet as a distinct creature rather than describing a person, action, or abstract idea. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary lexical meaning remains straightforward: hornet.

This Hebrew word means “bald,” describing a person whose head has lost its hair. It functions as a descriptive word for baldness rather than naming an action or an object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs three times in two verses, appearing in Leviticus and 2 Kings. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains a straightforward description of a bald head or person.

This Hebrew word functions as a personal name, identifying a person rather than expressing an ordinary descriptive meaning. It appears eight times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all in Ezra and Nehemiah. Its English rendering preserves it as a name, while the fallback term “the” does not by itself explain that naming function. The surrounding passage determines which individual is being identified, but the word’s normal role is to name a person in these historical records.

This Hebrew word means “moisten”: it describes making something damp or supplying it with moisture. It functions as an action word rather than naming an object or person. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezekiel 46:14. The surrounding verse determines exactly what is being moistened, but the word itself points to the action of making something moist. Its single occurrence means its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated biblical examples.

This Hebrew word refers to “sword” or “slaughter,” depending on how it is used in its sentence. It appears twice in the Old Testament, once rendered “sword” and once rendered “slaughter.” Thus, its central idea is connected with violent killing or the weapon associated with it, while the surrounding wording determines which sense is intended. It occurs in Psalm 42:10 and Ezekiel 21:22, but the precise force in either verse requires the verse and surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word refers to “desolation,” describing a state of emptiness, devastation, or abandonment. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Lamentations 3:47. Because the available material does not include the verse text, the word’s specific force in that passage must be understood from its surrounding context. Its basic sense remains clear: it names desolation rather than an action or person.

This Hebrew word refers to “destructions”—acts or conditions in which something is brought to ruin. It appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Psalm 107:20 and Lamentations 4:20. The word itself names destructive ruin, while the surrounding context determines the particular event or cause in each passage. Its meaning is therefore focused and concrete: destruction or ruin, rather than a broad description of every kind of trouble.

e.t: This Hebrew noun means “thorns,” referring to prickly growth that can hinder cultivation and make land difficult to work. It occurs seven times in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, all in Isaiah. The word appears in descriptions of neglected or difficult ground and in imagery involving burning or removal, presenting thorns as an obstacle or unwanted growth. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Prosperity is the meaning of this Hebrew word. It refers to a condition or state described as prosperity, functioning as a noun rather than an action or command. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Psalm 30:6, within this corpus. Since the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the word’s precise force in that sentence must be understood from its context in Psalm 30:6.

This Hebrew word refers to Ashdod or the people associated with Ashdod, a Philistine city. It functions as a place-related name, identifying the city itself in some passages and its inhabitants in others. In the Old Testament, it occurs six times across five verses, from Joshua through Nehemiah. The word is connected with Ashdod in accounts involving the ark of God and in references to the people of Ashdod. Its precise sense in a particular verse depends on whether the passage is naming the city or its people.

This Hebrew word means “Simeonites,” the people identified with Simeon. It functions as a group designation rather than a description of an action or quality. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs four times, appearing in Numbers, Joshua, and 1 Chronicles. Its precise reference in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its basic sense identifies the Simeonite people.

This Hebrew word describes an action that leaves something in “pieces.” It functions as a verb, expressing the dividing or breaking of a whole into separate parts. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in 1 Samuel 15:33, so its ordinary meaning is known from a single recorded use rather than a broad range of passages. The surrounding verse is needed to explain the particular action and its significance there; the word itself points to the result of something being left in “pieces.”

This Hebrew verb means “minister,” describing the act of serving or carrying out duties for another. It can refer to service in an official or sacred setting, including the work associated with priests and those appointed to assist in worship. The word occurs 98 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so its central idea is a recurring pattern of active service rather than a rare or specialized expression. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on who is being served and what duty is being performed.

This Hebrew word means “night.” It is a rare term in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing twice: once in Leviticus 11:16 and once in Deuteronomy 14:15. Both occurrences are rendered “night,” giving the clearest supported sense. Because verse text and surrounding passages are not included here, the word’s precise role in each listing cannot be explained further from this lexical entry alone.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “heap.” It is a noun used to name a heap as a thing, rather than an action or quality. In its five Old Testament occurrences, it refers to this kind of accumulated mass in passages from Deuteronomy, Joshua, and Jeremiah. The word’s exact force in any one verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its ordinary lexical sense remains a heap.

This Hebrew word refers to “secrets”: matters kept hidden rather than openly revealed. It names concealed knowledge or information, functioning as a term for what is not immediately known. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs three times, in Job and Psalms, including Job 11:6, Job 28:11, and Psalm 44:21. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

The available passage evidence connects Bigtha with the speech setting in Esther 1:10, but without the verse text here, the person’s specific role cannot be explained further. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Isaiah 28:16. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its connection with the words used there, but its basic sense remains “tried”: something subjected to testing and shown in relation to that testing.
